```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "85%")
find_proj_root <- function(path = getwd()) {
  path <- normalizePath(path)
  repeat {
    if (length(list.files(path, pattern = "\\.Rproj$"))) return(path)
    parent <- dirname(path)
    if (parent == path) stop("No .Rproj file found above ", getwd())
    path <- parent
  }
}
proj_root <- find_proj_root()
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = proj_root)

# cached chunks re-run whenever the data, the helpers or the Step 3 results change
file_md5 <- tools::md5sum(file.path(proj_root, c("data/processed/rq1_model_data.rds", "R/utils_models.R",
                                                 "outputs/models/rq1/rq1_step3_results.rds")))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(cache.extra = file_md5)
```

```{r load}
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "utils_data.R"))
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "utils_models.R"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(knitr)
  library(ranger)
})
N_CORES <- max(1, parallel::detectCores() - 1)

rq1 <- readRDS(file.path(paths$processed, "rq1_model_data.rds"))
dat <- rq1 |>
  filter(year >= 1996, !ta %in% c("Chatham Islands Territory", "Kawerau District")) |>
  droplevels()
train <- dat |> filter(split == "train")
test  <- dat |> filter(split == "test")

# same response, features and folds as Step 3
Y <- "rel_log_cost_m2"
num_main <- c("rel_house_m2", "log_houses_n", "multiunit_share", "apt_share", "retire_share",
              "dwell_per_1000", "houses_yoy", "log_resid_alt_real", "log_nonres_real")
fsets <- list(drivers  = c(num_main, "region", "is_city"),
              district = c(num_main, "ta"))
folds <- make_time_folds(train$year)

s3 <- readRDS(file.path(paths$models_rq1, "rq1_step3_results.rds"))
s3$chosen |> select(set, model, best_settings, cv_rmse) |> kable(digits = 4, caption = "Models chosen in Step 3")
```

# Purpose

Step 3 chose two models with the one-standard-error rule:

* a random forest on the **drivers** set (measured features plus region and city), and
* linear regression on the **district** set (measured features plus the district itself).

Step 3 told us *which* features matter. This notebook asks *how* they matter and where the models fail:

1. How does the prediction change as each driver changes (partial dependence)?
2. Do the drivers mean the same thing when we compare districts with each other as when we follow one district
   over time?
3. How much of each district's premium or discount is left once its drivers are accounted for?
4. Where and when are the test predictions wrong?
5. Would finer tuning have changed anything?

It ends with the answer to RQ1 and saves final models for later use (an app or poster).

The test set was already used once in Step 3. Nothing here changes a model because of test results: section 6
only describes the test errors, and section 7 uses cross-validation only.

# Refit the models on all training years

We refit three models on 1996–2019 at the settings Step 3 chose. Linear regression on the drivers set is not one
of the chosen models, but it gives a straight-line version of the same features to compare with the forest.

```{r refit}
rhs_of <- function(vars) paste(vars, collapse = " + ")
fml_of <- function(y, vars) as.formula(paste(y, "~", rhs_of(vars)))
best <- s3$best_settings

# random forest, drivers set (chosen)
b_rf <- best[["Random forest"]]$drivers
rf_drv <- ranger(fml_of(Y, fsets$drivers), data = train, num.trees = 500,
                 mtry = b_rf$mtry, min.node.size = b_rf$min.node.size,
                 num.threads = N_CORES, seed = 462)

# linear regression, drivers set (straight-line comparison) and district set (chosen)
fit_lm <- function(vars, data = train) list(fit = lm(fml_of(Y, vars), data = data), rhs = rhs_of(vars))
predict_lm <- function(m, newdata) as.numeric(predict(m$fit, newdata = newdata))

lm_drv  <- fit_lm(fsets$drivers)
lm_dist <- fit_lm(fsets$district)

# one prediction function per model, so the code below treats them alike
pred_funs <- list(
  "Random forest, drivers" = function(d) predict(rf_drv, d, num.threads = N_CORES)$predictions,
  "Linear, drivers"        = function(d) predict_lm(lm_drv, d),
  "Linear, district"       = function(d) predict_lm(lm_dist, d))

# check: the refitted models reproduce the Step 3 test RMSE
step3_rmse <- s3$test |> filter((model == "Random forest" & set == "drivers") |
                                 (model == "Linear regression" & set %in% c("drivers", "district"))) |>
  transmute(model = sub("Linear regression", "Linear", paste0(model, ", ", set)), step3 = test_rmse)
tibble(model = names(pred_funs),
       refit = map_dbl(pred_funs, \(f) reg_metrics(test[[Y]], f(test))$rmse)) |>
  left_join(step3_rmse, by = "model") |> kable(digits = 4, caption = "Test RMSE: refit vs Step 3")
```

**Observation.** The refitted models give the same test RMSE as Step 3, so the plots below describe the models
that were actually evaluated.

# How each driver changes the prediction (partial dependence)

A **partial dependence plot** shows how a model's average prediction changes as one feature moves, with all other
features kept at their observed values. For each value *v* on a grid we set that feature to *v* in every training
row, predict, and average. The result is the model's view of that feature's effect, averaged over everything else.

We use the 5th to 95th percentile of each feature, since the tails have few rows. Curves are centred at zero, so
the y-axis reads as "% dearer or cheaper than the model's average prediction".

```{r pdp-fun}
# partial dependence of one feature: average prediction with the feature fixed at each grid value
partial_dependence <- function(pred_fun, data, var, grid) {
  map_dbl(grid, function(v) {
    data[[var]] <- v
    mean(pred_fun(data))
  })
}

pdp_vars <- c("log_resid_alt_real", "dwell_per_1000", "log_houses_n",
              "rel_house_m2", "log_nonres_real", "houses_yoy")

# labels, and how to show each feature's values in natural units in the panel titles
pdp_labels <- tribble(
  ~feature,             ~label,                                    ~fmt,
  "log_resid_alt_real", "Residential alterations ($ per quarter)", \(x) paste0("$", signif(expm1(x) / 1e6, 2), "m"),
  "dwell_per_1000",     "New dwellings per 1,000 residents",       \(x) as.character(round(x, 1)),
  "log_houses_n",       "New houses in the quarter",               \(x) as.character(round(exp(x))),
  "rel_house_m2",       "House size vs rest of NZ",                \(x) sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * (exp(x) - 1)),
  "log_nonres_real",    "New non-residential work ($ per quarter)", \(x) paste0("$", signif(expm1(x) / 1e6, 2), "m"),
  "houses_yoy",         "Houses vs same quarter last year",        \(x) sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * (exp(x) - 1))
)
pdp_probs <- seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05)
```

```{r pdp, cache = TRUE}
pdp <- expand_grid(model = names(pred_funs), feature = pdp_vars) |>
  pmap_dfr(function(model, feature) {
    grid <- quantile(train[[feature]], pdp_probs, names = FALSE)
    yhat <- partial_dependence(pred_funs[[model]], train, feature, grid)
    tibble(model, feature, pctile = pdp_probs, value = grid, yhat)
  }) |>
  group_by(model, feature) |>
  mutate(effect = yhat - mean(yhat)) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r pdp-plot, fig.height = 6, out.width = "100%"}
# panel title: feature name and its 5th-95th percentile range in natural units
panel_titles <- pdp_labels |>
  mutate(range = map2_chr(feature, fmt, \(v, f) paste(f(quantile(train[[v]], c(0.05, 0.95))), collapse = " to ")),
         title = paste0(label, "\n(", range, ")"))

p_pdp <- pdp |>
  left_join(panel_titles |> select(feature, title), by = "feature") |>
  mutate(title = factor(title, levels = panel_titles$title)) |>
  ggplot(aes(100 * pctile, 100 * effect, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~title, ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Random forest, drivers" = "#2a6f97", "Linear, drivers" = "#9aa5b1",
                                 "Linear, district" = "#e76f51")) +
  labs(title = "How the predicted relative cost changes as each driver increases",
       subtitle = "Partial dependence, centred at zero. x = percentile of the feature among training rows",
       x = "Percentile of the feature (5th to 95th)", y = "Effect on relative cost (%)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text = element_text(size = 8.5))
save_fig(p_pdp, "fig24_partial_dependence", height = 6, width = 9)
```

```{r effect-table}
# size of each effect: change in prediction from the 10th to the 90th percentile of the feature
effect_10_90 <- expand_grid(model = names(pred_funs), feature = pdp_vars) |>
  pmap_dfr(function(model, feature) {
    q <- quantile(train[[feature]], c(0.1, 0.9), names = FALSE)
    change <- diff(partial_dependence(pred_funs[[model]], train, feature, q))
    tibble(model, feature, change)
  }) |>
  mutate(change_pct = 100 * (exp(change) - 1)) |>
  select(-change) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = change_pct) |>
  left_join(pdp_labels |> select(feature, label), by = "feature") |>
  relocate(label, .after = feature)
save_tab(effect_10_90, "t12_effect_sizes") |>
  kable(digits = 1, caption = "Change in predicted relative cost (%) from the 10th to the 90th percentile of each feature")
```

**Observation.** The table gives the change from a typical low value (10th percentile) to a typical high value
(90th percentile) of each feature.

* **Residential alteration spending** has the largest and most consistent effect. All three models agree: moving
  from the 10th to the 90th percentile raises the predicted relative cost by about
  `r sprintf("%+.1f", effect_10_90[["Random forest, drivers"]][effect_10_90$feature == "log_resid_alt_real"])`% (forest) to `r sprintf("%+.1f", effect_10_90[["Linear, drivers"]][effect_10_90$feature == "log_resid_alt_real"])`% (linear).
  The forest's curve is close to a straight line, so the linear models describe this driver well.
* **New dwellings per 1,000 residents** adds `r sprintf("%+.1f", effect_10_90[["Random forest, drivers"]][effect_10_90$feature == "dwell_per_1000"])`%
  between the 10th and 90th percentile in the forest, and the forest's curve then jumps by about another 4% in the
  fastest-growing tenth (more than about 11 new dwellings per 1,000 residents a year). A straight line cannot bend
  like this, so the linear model spreads the effect evenly instead.
* **Number of new houses** is where the models disagree. The drivers-set linear model says more houses means cheaper
  (`r sprintf("%+.1f", effect_10_90[["Linear, drivers"]][effect_10_90$feature == "log_houses_n"])`%). The district-set linear model says the opposite (`r sprintf("%+.1f", effect_10_90[["Linear, district"]][effect_10_90$feature == "log_houses_n"])`%).
  The forest shows almost no overall effect. Section 4 explains why.
* **House size**, **non-residential work** and **year-on-year change in houses** each move the prediction by 2% or
  less. Houses bigger than the rest of NZ are slightly cheaper per m², as expected from fixed costs (kitchens,
  bathrooms, consents) being spread over more floor area, but the effect is small.

Most effects are a few percent, small next to the ±15–20% gaps between the dearest and cheapest districts. The
measured drivers shift a district's cost at the margin. They do not explain most of the gap between places.

## Do two drivers work together? (interaction)

The tree in Step 3 split first on alteration spending and then on growth, which suggests the two act together.
A two-way partial dependence plot fixes both features on a grid and averages the forest's predictions.

```{r pdp2, cache = TRUE}
g_alt  <- quantile(train$log_resid_alt_real, seq(0.05, 0.95, length.out = 10), names = FALSE)
g_grow <- quantile(train$dwell_per_1000,     seq(0.05, 0.95, length.out = 10), names = FALSE)
pdp2 <- expand_grid(alt = g_alt, grow = g_grow) |>
  mutate(yhat = map2_dbl(alt, grow, function(a, g) {
    d <- train; d$log_resid_alt_real <- a; d$dwell_per_1000 <- g
    mean(pred_funs[["Random forest, drivers"]](d))
  }))
```

```{r pdp2-plot, fig.height = 4.2}
p_pdp2 <- pdp2 |>
  mutate(effect = 100 * (yhat - mean(yhat)),
         alt_m = factor(signif(expm1(alt) / 1e6, 2)), grow = factor(round(grow, 1))) |>
  ggplot(aes(alt_m, grow, fill = effect)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%+.0f", effect)), size = 2.8) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2a6f97", mid = "white", high = "#e76f51", midpoint = 0) +
  labs(title = "Random forest: alteration spending and growth together",
       subtitle = "Two-way partial dependence; numbers = % above or below the average prediction",
       x = "Residential alterations ($m per quarter)", y = "New dwellings per 1,000 residents",
       fill = "Effect (%)")
save_fig(p_pdp2, "fig25_interaction_alterations_growth", height = 4.2, width = 8)
```

**Observation.** The two drivers reinforce each other. With low alteration spending, growth barely matters
(the left columns are all about −3% to −5%). With high alteration spending, fast growth adds a lot: the top-right
corner is about +14%, while high spending with slow growth is about +3%. The dearest new houses are found where both
are true: a wealthy market with a lot of renovation work *and* rapid population growth. Queenstown-Lakes is the
clearest example. A model with only additive terms (OLS, GAM) cannot represent this, which is one reason the forest
beat them on the drivers set.

# Comparing districts versus following one district over time

The drivers set has no district variable, so its coefficients mix two comparisons. One is *between* districts
(is a busy district dearer than a quiet one?). The other is *within* a district over time (is a district dearer in
its busy quarters?). Once the district is in the model, every district gets its own level, and the remaining
coefficients describe only the within-district comparison.

Comparing the standardised linear-regression coefficients of the two sets shows which drivers change meaning.

```{r within-between}
std_coef <- function(m, data) {
  b <- coef(m$fit)[num_main]
  tibble(feature = num_main, coef = b * map_dbl(num_main, \(v) sd(data[[v]])))
}
within_between <- std_coef(lm_drv, train) |> rename(`drivers set (between + within)` = coef) |>
  left_join(std_coef(lm_dist, train) |> rename(`district set (within only)` = coef), by = "feature") |>
  mutate(`sign flips` = sign(`drivers set (between + within)`) != sign(`district set (within only)`)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(`drivers set (between + within)`)))
save_tab(within_between, "t13_within_between") |>
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Linear regression, standardised coefficients (log points per 1 SD of the feature)")
```

**Observation.** Two drivers change meaning once the district is held fixed.

* **Number of new houses** flips sign. *Between* districts, places that build many houses are cheaper per m² than
  places with the same alteration spending and growth that build fewer (volume builders, large subdivisions such
  as Selwyn). On its own, without alteration spending in the model, the number of houses has a small positive
  link with cost, because both measure how big a district's building market is (correlation 0.84). *Within* a district, its busier quarters are dearer
  (more demand for the same builders and materials). The drivers-set model mixes the two, and the between-district
  pattern dominates. This also explains the flat forest curve in section 3: the forest combines the two opposite
  patterns.
* **Dwellings per 1,000 residents** shrinks from 0.031 to 0.003. Fast-growing *districts* are dearer, but a
  district is not much dearer in its own fast-growth years. The growth effect is mostly a difference between places.

Alteration spending keeps the same sign and a similar size in both sets, so it holds both between and within
districts. The mix shares (apartments, retirement units, multi-unit) are close to zero in both, and their sign
flips are noise.

# How much of each district's premium do the drivers explain?

In the district-set linear model, each district has its own coefficient. That coefficient is the part of the
district's relative cost that its measured drivers do **not** explain. We compare it with the district's raw
average relative cost over 1996–2019. Both are centred on the average district so they are on the same footing.
There is no shrinkage, so the premiums of small districts, estimated from few quarters, are the noisiest.

```{r premium}
b_dist <- coef(lm_dist$fit)
ta_levels <- levels(train$ta)
premium <- tibble(ta = ta_levels,
                  after = c(0, b_dist[paste0("ta", ta_levels[-1])])) |>   # first level is the reference (0)
  left_join(train |> group_by(ta) |> summarise(raw = mean(rel_log_cost_m2), quarters = n()) |>
              mutate(ta = as.character(ta)), by = "ta") |>
  mutate(after = after - mean(after), raw = raw - mean(raw),
         explained = raw - after)

premium_show <- bind_rows(premium |> slice_max(after, n = 10), premium |> slice_min(after, n = 10)) |>
  mutate(name = fct_reorder(str_remove(ta, " District| City"), after))

p_prem <- premium_show |>
  pivot_longer(c(raw, after), names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(measure = recode(measure, raw = "Raw average", after = "After accounting for drivers")) |>
  ggplot(aes(100 * value, name)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(aes(group = name), colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = measure), size = 2.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Raw average" = "#9aa5b1", "After accounting for drivers" = "#e76f51")) +
  labs(title = "Location premium before and after the measured drivers",
       subtitle = "Ten dearest and ten cheapest districts after drivers (linear regression, district set, 1996–2019)",
       x = "Relative cost vs the average district (%)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
save_fig(p_prem, "fig26_district_premium", height = 5.5, width = 8)

c(sd_raw = sd(premium$raw), sd_after = sd(premium$after),
  share_of_spread_left = var(premium$after) / var(premium$raw))
```

**Observation.** The measured drivers explain only part of why some districts are dear.

* The spread of district premiums falls only from `r fmt_pct(sd(premium$raw), 1)` to `r fmt_pct(sd(premium$after), 1)`
  (standard deviation, log scale). About `r fmt_pct(1 - var(premium$after) / var(premium$raw), 0)` of the variance
  between district averages is explained by the drivers; the rest is location itself.
* **Queenstown-Lakes** stays the dearest district even after its drivers (about +15% vs the average district).
  **Thames-Coromandel** and **Wellington City** lose about half their premium: their high alteration spending
  accounts for that part.
* **Auckland and Christchurch** move from dearer than average to cheaper than their drivers predict. They have the
  largest alteration and non-residential spending in the country, so the model expects them to be very dear, and
  they are less dear than that. This shows a weakness in our features: the activity measures are **total dollars**,
  so they partly measure district *size*. Per-resident versions would separate size from wealth (see the
  limitations in section 8).
* **Selwyn, Hamilton and Horowhenua** remain cheap after their drivers. These are flat, easy-to-build greenfield
  markets with volume builders, which our features do not capture directly.

# Where are the test predictions wrong?

We use the test predictions saved in Step 3 for the two chosen models and the district-mean baseline. A residual
here is *predicted minus actual*, so a negative residual means the model under-predicted.

```{r test-preds}
tp <- s3$test_predictions |>
  mutate(model = paste0(model, ", ", set)) |>
  filter(model %in% c("Random forest, drivers", "Linear regression, district", "District mean, none")) |>
  mutate(model = recode(model, "District mean, none" = "District mean (baseline)",
                        "Linear regression, district" = "Linear, district"),
         resid = pred - obs) |>
  left_join(test |> mutate(row = row_number()) |> select(row, houses_n), by = "row")
```

## By year

```{r by-year, fig.height = 3.6}
by_year <- tp |>
  group_by(model, year) |>
  summarise(rmse = sqrt(mean(resid^2)), bias = mean(resid), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(test |> group_by(year) |> summarise(spread = sd(.data[[Y]])), by = "year")

p_year <- by_year |>
  ggplot(aes(year, rmse, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = spread, colour = "Spread of actual values (SD)"), linetype = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Random forest, drivers" = "#2a6f97", "Linear, district" = "#e76f51",
                                 "District mean (baseline)" = "#9aa5b1",
                                 "Spread of actual values (SD)" = "grey30")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2020:2026) +
  labs(title = "Test error by year",
       subtitle = "Errors grow after 2023, along with the spread between districts. 2026 has two quarters only.",
       x = NULL, y = "RMSE (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
save_fig(p_year, "fig27_test_error_by_year", height = 3.6, width = 8.5)

by_year |> select(model, year, rmse, bias) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = c(rmse, bias)) |> kable(digits = 3)
```

**Observation.** All three models have their smallest errors in 2020–2022 and their largest in 2024, the year the
spread between districts peaked (dashed line). The linear model beats the district-mean baseline in 2020–2023 and
falls slightly behind it in 2024–2026. The relationships learned before 2020 held for a few years and then started
to drift.

Every model under-predicts on average (negative bias, about −2% early on and −4% by 2025–26). The average relative
cost of the modelled districts rose after 2020: smaller districts became dearer compared with the large centres
that dominate the "rest of NZ" average. A model trained on 1996–2019 has no way to know this.

## By number of houses

```{r by-size, fig.height = 3.4}
by_size <- tp |>
  mutate(size = cut(houses_n, c(4, 9, 24, 49, 99, Inf),
                    labels = c("5–9", "10–24", "25–49", "50–99", "100+"))) |>
  group_by(model, size) |>
  summarise(rows = n(), rmse = sqrt(mean(resid^2)), .groups = "drop")

p_size <- ggplot(by_size, aes(size, rmse, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Random forest, drivers" = "#2a6f97", "Linear, district" = "#e76f51",
                               "District mean (baseline)" = "#9aa5b1")) +
  labs(title = "Errors are largest where few houses are built",
       x = "New houses in the district-quarter", y = "Test RMSE (log scale)", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
save_fig(p_size, "fig28_test_error_by_size", height = 3.4)

by_size |> filter(model == "Linear, district") |> select(size, rows, rmse) |> kable(digits = 3)
```

**Observation.** Error falls steadily as the number of houses rises: RMSE is about
`r round(by_size$rmse[by_size$model == "Linear, district" & by_size$size == "5–9"], 2)` for district-quarters with 5–9
houses and `r round(by_size$rmse[by_size$model == "Linear, district" & by_size$size == "100+"], 2)` for those with 100 or
more. This is the same funnel as in Step 1: with few houses, one unusual consent moves the quarter's $/m². Part of
the test error is therefore noise in the response that no model could remove.

## By district

```{r by-district}
by_district <- tp |>
  filter(model == "Linear, district") |>
  group_by(ta) |>
  summarise(quarters = n(), median_houses = median(houses_n),
            mean_resid = mean(resid), rmse = sqrt(mean(resid^2)), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(rmse))
save_tab(by_district, "t14_test_error_by_district") |>
  head(10) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Linear regression (district set): ten districts with the largest test RMSE")
```

**Observation.** Two groups stand out.

* **Small districts** (Ōpōtiki, Wairoa, Otorohanga, Waimate) with a median of 6–9 houses a quarter. Their errors are
  mostly noise, as the previous section showed.
* **Larger districts that changed after 2020.** Coastal and lifestyle districts (Kaipara, Thames-Coromandel,
  Western Bay of Plenty, Queenstown-Lakes) were under-predicted by 12–15%: they became even dearer relative to the
  rest of NZ. Waimakariri, a volume-building district north of Christchurch, was over-predicted by about 14%: it
  became cheaper. These look like real shifts in the market after COVID (more demand for lifestyle and holiday
  areas, more volume building in Canterbury) rather than model errors that better tuning could fix.

# Would finer tuning change anything?

Step 3 searched a coarse grid. Here we search a finer grid around the forest's chosen settings, using the same
training folds. Linear regression has no settings to refine. We only look at CV scores, because
the test set has been used.

```{r refine, cache = TRUE}
fp_rf <- function(vars, y) function(tr, nw, p)
  predict(ranger(fml_of(y, vars), data = tr, num.trees = 500, mtry = p$mtry,
                 min.node.size = p$min.node.size, num.threads = N_CORES, seed = 462), data = nw)$predictions
rf_fine <- cv_tune(fp_rf(fsets$drivers, Y),
                   expand_grid(mtry = 5:8, min.node.size = c(10, 15, 20, 30)),
                   train, folds, Y)
```

```{r refine-table}
rf_step3 <- s3$cv |> filter(model == "Random forest", set == "drivers")
rf_fine$summary |> head(5) |> select(mtry, min.node.size, cv_rmse, cv_rmse_sd) |>
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Finer forest grid, best five settings")
c(step3_cv_rmse = rf_step3$cv_rmse, step3_se = rf_step3$cv_rmse_se,
  refined_cv_rmse = rf_fine$best$cv_rmse,
  gain = rf_step3$cv_rmse - rf_fine$best$cv_rmse)
```

**Observation.** The finer grid picks the same setting as Step 3 (`mtry` = 6, `min.node.size` = 20), and the
top five settings are within 0.0001 of each other, far less than one standard error
(`r round(rf_step3$cv_rmse_se, 4)`). The forest is not sensitive to its settings near the optimum, so further tuning
would not change any conclusion. We keep the Step 3 models.

# Answer to RQ1

**Question.** What drives the real cost per m² of new houses across New Zealand districts?

**Short answer.** Location matters most. The measured drivers explain a modest part of it, led by how much a
district spends on renovating existing homes and how fast it is growing.

| Driver | Direction | Size (10th → 90th percentile) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Residential alteration spending | dearer | about +8% to +11% | top feature in all three importance methods; same sign between and within districts |
| Region (broad location) | varies | up to about ±10% | second in importance in Step 3 |
| Dwellings per 1,000 residents | dearer | about +3% to +6%, plus about +4% more in the fastest-growing 10% | differs *between* districts, little *within* |
| Number of new houses | cheaper between districts (for the same alteration spending), dearer within | about ±5–6% | volume markets are cheaper; busy quarters are dearer |
| Relative house size | slightly cheaper | about −1% to −2% | fixed costs spread over more floor area |
| Dwelling mix (apartments, townhouses, retirement) | none detected | under 1% | near zero in every model |

**How well can we predict it?**

* With the measured drivers and broad region only, the best models (random forest, XGBoost, SVM) explain about a
  third of the variation in relative cost (CV R² ≈ 0.32). That is about as much as knowing the district name alone.
* With the district added, linear regression explains about 38% in cross-validation and predicts 2020–2026 within about
  8% (MAPE), marginally better than each district's historical average.
* About 85% of the variation between district averages is not explained by our measured drivers. It sits in
  location itself: land, terrain, local labour markets, and the kind of house each place builds.

**Limitations.**

* Our activity features are total dollars, so they partly measure district size. Per-resident versions (alterations
  per resident, non-residential per resident) would be cleaner. Population estimates were not in this release.
* We do not observe land prices, house quality or specification, or builder type, which are the most likely sources
  of the unexplained location premium.
* The data are observational. "Dearer where alteration spending is high" is an association, not a cause; both
  probably reflect wealthier markets.
* Relationships drifted after 2023 (section 6.1), so a model for current use should be retrained regularly.

# Save final models

For later use (an app or the poster), we refit the two chosen models on **all** modelled rows from 1996 to
2026Q2. The test years have done their job, and the final models should learn from the most recent data. We
also save the latest values of every feature for each district, which an app can use as default inputs, and the
latest "rest of NZ" $/m², which turns a relative prediction back into dollars.

```{r save-final}
final_rf <- ranger(fml_of(Y, fsets$drivers), data = dat, num.trees = 500,
                   mtry = b_rf$mtry, min.node.size = b_rf$min.node.size,
                   num.threads = N_CORES, seed = 462)
final_lm <- fit_lm(fsets$district, data = dat)

# latest four quarters for each district: average feature values and the rest-of-NZ $/m²
latest <- dat |>
  group_by(ta) |>
  slice_max(t_index, n = 4) |>
  summarise(region = first(region), is_city = first(is_city),
            across(all_of(num_main), mean),
            loo_cost_m2 = mean(loo_cost_m2), real_cost_m2 = mean(real_cost_m2),
            last_quarter = max(as.character(yq)), .groups = "drop")

saveRDS(list(rf_drivers = final_rf, lm_district = final_lm,
             features = fsets, num_main = num_main, response = Y,
             factor_levels = list(ta = levels(dat$ta), region = levels(dat$region)),
             latest = latest, trained_on = "1996Q1-2026Q2, districts with >= 5 new houses"),
        file.path(paths$models_rq1, "rq1_final_models.rds"))
file.size(file.path(paths$models_rq1, "rq1_final_models.rds")) / 2^20   # MB
```
